note: The words that recur in the project's map, explained from scratch. Each entry: aliases to recognize in the text, a title, an explanation, and related terms. Used by tools/status_html.py.

entries.title: Token
entries.text: The piece of text the model reasons with: usually a short word, a chunk of a long word, or a punctuation mark. «inference» can be two tokens, «the» one. The model does not see letters: it sees a sequence of numbers, one per token.

entries.title: Tokenizer
entries.text: The piece that translates text into tokens and back. It must give exactly the same numbers as the model's original tokenizer: if it gets even a piece wrong, the model reads a different sentence than the one you wrote.

entries.title: Prompt
entries.text: Everything you feed the model before it starts answering: the question, the file it has read, the conversation so far. The longer it is, the more work there is before the first word of the answer.

entries.title: Prefill (reading the prompt)
entries.text: The first phase: the model reads the whole prompt at once and builds the memory of that text. All the tokens together, so the cores work full and it is the «fat» phase. In Trochilus it is also the phase where, if the model does not fit in RAM, the whole disk cost is paid.

entries.title: Decode (generation)
entries.text: The second phase: the model produces one token at a time, and each one depends on the one before, so they cannot be done in parallel. It is «thin» work: all the weights get reread to produce a single word, so the bottleneck is memory speed, not the cores.

entries.title: Context
entries.text: How much text the model is holding in mind at that moment: prompt plus response. The bigger it grows, the bigger the context memory (the KV) becomes and the more every new token costs, because it has to look back over all of it.

entries.title: Attention
entries.text: The mechanism by which, to write the new token, the model looks at every token before it and decides how much weight to give each. It is why the model understands what a «he» written twenty lines up refers to, and it is also why a long context costs so much.

entries.title: KV (the context memory)
entries.text: For every token already read the model saves two vectors — key and value — so it does not have to redo the math over the whole text at every new word. It is a kind of already-chewed summary of what it has seen. It grows with the context and gets read in full at every token, so how it sits in memory matters a lot.

entries.title: MoE (mixture-of-experts model)
entries.text: A model made of many specialized pieces instead of one single block. For each token it uses only a few — in our case 8 out of 64 per layer — so it is huge on disk but computes like a small one. The flip side: you do not know in advance which pieces you will need.

entries.title: Expert
entries.text: One of the model's specialized pieces: in practice three matrices of numbers. In our model there are 64 per layer, 1024 in all, and each weighs 6.375 MiB — they are what takes up almost all of the model file.

entries.title: Router
entries.text: The piece that, for every token and every layer, picks which 8 experts to use. It is small and fast, but it is the one deciding what will need to be read from disk: hence the idea of peeking at its choices ahead of time.

entries.title: Layer
entries.text: One stratum of the model. The token passes through the layers one after another, and at each step its representation is refined. Our model has 16 of them, and each has its own 64 experts.

entries.title: Logit
entries.text: The scores the model gives to every possible word before picking one: 50 304 numbers, one for each token in the vocabulary. They are the raw result, before any choice: if two versions of the engine give identical logits, they are doing exactly the same thing.

entries.title: Identical to the byte
entries.text: Not «roughly the same»: the exact same numbers, bit for bit. It is the project's yardstick — a fast version of a computation is kept only if it gives the same bits as the slow one. That way a speedup can never quietly worsen the quality of the answers.

entries.title: Quantization
entries.text: Writing the model's weights with fewer digits so they take up less space: from 4 bytes to 1 (Q8_0), or even less (Q4). Fewer bytes means less disk to read and less RAM, but the numbers are no longer exact, so the answers can shift a little. That is why in this project it is a mode you opt into, never the default behavior.

entries.title: GGUF
entries.text: The file format a ready-to-use model comes in: a single file with all the weights and the information to interpret them. It is the standard born with llama.cpp, and reading it is the engine's front door.

entries.title: Expert budget
entries.text: How much RAM we give the experts' pantry. Full budget: the model sits entirely in memory. Half budget: half in memory, the rest fetched from disk when needed. This is how a model bigger than RAM can still run.

entries.title: LRU (whoever is not used, leaves)
entries.text: The rule for deciding who to throw out when the pantry is full: out goes whoever has not been used the longest (Least Recently Used). It works because the past resembles the future: two nearby tokens almost always ask for the same experts, 3.6 out of 8 on average. It is the same rule by which you keep on your desk the books you are consulting and put the others back on the shelf.

entries.title: Cache
entries.text: A stash of stuff kept close because it will be used again. There are two kinds here: our own pantry of experts in RAM, and the one the operating system keeps on its own for every file it reads. The second one, in measurements, is a problem: it makes the disk look as fast as RAM.

entries.title: Direct read
entries.text: Asking the operating system to read from disk without keeping a copy for itself. It serves two purposes: not having the model in RAM twice, and measuring the real disk instead of its copy in memory — without it, the prompt would look 2.42 times faster than it really is.

entries.title: NVMe disk
entries.text: The laptop's solid-state disk. Fast compared to a mechanical disk, extremely slow compared to RAM: ~1.5 GB/s against RAM's ~57 GB/s, that is, almost forty times less. That is why, if the model does not fit in RAM, the disk becomes the bottleneck of everything.

entries.title: Memory bandwidth
entries.text: How many bytes per second can be read. It matters more than raw compute power in this engine: generating a token mostly means dragging weights from memory to the cores, and the cores end up waiting. This machine's RAM does ~57 GB/s, the disk ~1.5.

entries.title: tok/s (tokens per second)
entries.text: The engine's speed. In the prompt it is tokens read per second (hundreds), in generation it is tokens produced per second (tens). Two different numbers that do not compare to each other: reading is much faster than writing.

entries.title: Threads and cores
entries.text: Cores are the processor's compute units (this machine has 16 real ones), threads are the jobs that run on them. The pool is the team of threads already up and ready, so their wake-up cost is not paid every time. More threads does not always mean faster: in generation, past 8, they all end up waiting on memory.

entries.title: SIMD (vector instructions)
entries.text: Instructions that do the same math on 8 or 16 numbers in one go, instead of one at a time. That is where most of the kernels' speed comes from. Every processor has a different set of them, so the engine carries several versions and picks one at runtime.

entries.title: Kernel
entries.text: Not the operating system's kind here: it is a small function that does one computation repeated millions of times — multiplying a row of weights by a vector. It is the hottest piece of the engine, the one rewritten in SIMD or assembly for 10-20 times the speed.

entries.title: Tier
entries.text: The rung of instructions a CPU can do (scalar, AVX2, AVX-512). The engine tries them all in its tests and picks the best one at startup, on whatever machine it finds: it runs on a brand-new laptop the same as on one ten years old, with the same result.

entries.title: Hot zone / profile zones
entries.text: «Hot zone» is the code that runs on every token, where nothing is allocated and no strings are written: there, even a tiny thing costs. The profile's «zones», instead, are the pieces we split the time into (attention, experts, router, weight reads) to know where it goes.

entries.title: Profile
entries.text: The measurement of where the time goes inside a run, zone by zone. It keeps optimization from being done by guesswork: first look at which piece weighs the most, then touch that one. It was a profile that revealed the prompt was rereading the experts at every pass.

entries.title: Median, spread, A/A
entries.text: How measurement works in this project: never a single run. N runs are made and the middle value is taken (median), how much they swing is stated (spread), and the very same thing is also measured twice (A/A) to know the background noise. A gain only counts if it is bigger than the noise.

entries.title: Still machine
entries.text: Measurements are taken when the computer is not doing anything else: no containers running, no leftover processes of ours. Every session logs how busy the machine was, because with the wrong load the numbers lie, and so do the conclusions.

entries.title: Oracle
entries.text: The comparison against the truth: the same inputs given to transformers (the Python reference implementation) and to our engine, and the results must match. It runs on tiny, purpose-built models, so it is fast and fits inside the automated tests.

entries.title: Mutation
entries.text: The test of the tests: the code is broken on purpose, at one precise spot, and we look at whether any test notices. If they all stay green, that test was not checking anything. It is how you avoid a safety net full of holes.

entries.title: KL (how differently two models think)
entries.text: A number telling how far one model's prediction diverges from another's on the same text. Zero: identical. Below 0.01: negligible difference. Above 1: they are saying different things. It is used to judge the inexact modes, where the bits do not match by construction.

entries.title: Speculative decoding
entries.text: Instead of producing one token at a time, several are guessed at once in a block (for instance copying them from a piece of text already seen) and then all checked together in a single pass. The right ones are kept, the rest thrown away: the result is identical, but when the text repeats — as in code — it is faster.

entries.title: Sanitizer
entries.text: Versions of the program compiled with extra checks that make memory errors (ASan) or data races between threads (TSan) blow up right away. They are very slow, so they never ship: they run in the tests, where they catch bugs that would otherwise show up at random, months later.

entries.title: Slot store
entries.text: The pantry itself: a chunk of RAM divided into slots the size of one expert, allocated once at startup. When an expert that is missing is needed, it is read from disk into a free slot (or one freed by the LRU). No allocation during generation: that is a hot zone.

entries.title: Pass (prompt block)
entries.text: The prompt is not processed all at once but in groups of 512 tokens: each group goes through every layer, then it is the next group's turn. It is done this way to avoid keeping too many intermediate results in RAM — and it is exactly this that, under budget, makes the experts get reread from disk at every group.
